before.description: Perplexity is an AI-powered answer engine that returns cited, up-to-date sources instead of a list of links, with an agentic Deep Research mode and multi-model access to systems from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
before.description_long:
Perplexity is a conversational search tool that answers questions with cited, up-to-date sources instead of a list of links. It sits somewhere between a chatbot and a search engine, and over 2026 it has leaned hard into research and agentic work.

The headline feature is Advanced Deep Research. It runs agentically inside Perplexity's Computer assistant, asks clarifying questions before it starts, accepts follow-ups mid-run, and shows live source and progress tracking. On Pro and Max, Deep Research is powered by models from Anthropic.

Beyond research, Perplexity gives you multi-model access to systems from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and other vendors, a Model Council feature that compares several models side by side on the same question, and the Comet browser for AI-assisted browsing.

Pricing is structured in tiers. Free costs $0 a month. Pro is listed at $17 a month when billed annually, and includes 4,000 bonus Computer credits; a separate monthly-billing price is not published on the site. Max is listed at $167 a month when billed annually and includes 10,000 monthly Computer credits, Model Council, Sora 2 Pro video and Nano Banana Pro image generation, and unlimited Labs. An Enterprise plan is also listed, with pricing available on request.

The limitations are worth knowing. Like any AI system it can still misread or over-trust weak sources, so citations need checking. The site only publishes annual-billing rates for Pro and Max, so there is no visible month-to-month option above the free tier, the free tier itself is limited for frequent use, and agentic Computer work is metered by a monthly credit budget that heavy users can exhaust. Juggling multiple models plus Model Council also adds a learning curve.

Perplexity is a strong pick if you do a lot of source-backed research, want agentic Deep Research, or like comparing several AI models on the same question. Casual users who just need a few answers a day can stay on Free, while heavier users should expect to commit to an annual Pro or Max plan.

before.description: Suno is an AI music generator that turns a text prompt into a full song with vocals and instruments. The current model is v6 (with a v6-wild variant) on paid plans, while free accounts run the lighter v6-mini model.
before.description_long:
Suno is a text-to-music tool that writes, arranges and performs a song from a short description or your own lyrics. You type a prompt, pick a style, and it returns finished tracks with vocals and backing instrumentation in about a minute.

The current model is v6, launched September 9, 2026 and described by Suno as developed with industry partners including Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe. Paid plans run v6 and v6-wild; the free plan runs the lighter v6-mini. Prior model versions are being retired.

Day to day, the tool covers the full loop: generation from a prompt, custom lyrics, style and persona control, Voices for recording or uploading your own singing voice, Custom Models that fine-tune the system to your own catalogue (Pro and Premier), stem separation on paid plans, and audio upload to extend or remix existing material. Premier also includes Suno Studio, with MIDI, effects and automation tools.

Pricing runs on a credit system. Free is $0 per month with 50 credits per day for personal, non-commercial use, no stem separation, 8-minute uploads, and no regular monthly song downloads (accounts that joined before September 3, 2026 may get limited lifetime trial downloads). Pro is $10 per month, or $8 per month billed annually ($96 per year), for 2,500 credits a month, 20 song downloads a month, commercial use rights, two stem types, 30-minute uploads and a priority queue. Premier is $30 per month, or $24 per month billed annually ($288 per year), for 10,000 credits a month, 60 song downloads a month (unlimited inside Suno Studio), commercial use, three stem types and Suno Studio.

The main limitations are that regular downloads are no longer part of the free plan, so testing the output beyond streaming requires a paid subscription, and even paid plans cap downloads per month. Suno is also facing active litigation: a US federal judge in Massachusetts denied its motion to dismiss copyright and DMCA claims on September 28, 2026, which adds uncertainty around commercial use.

Suno suits hobbyists experimenting with ideas and musicians who want fast demos or reference tracks, and content creators who need commercial-use tracks and are willing to pay for a plan with enough monthly downloads and accept the current legal uncertainty.

before.description: Synthesia is an AI video platform that turns text scripts into narrated videos with realistic avatars. The current release, Synthesia 3.0, introduces the Express-2 full-body avatar engine with natural hand and body gestures, along with interactive Video Agents.
before.description_long:
Synthesia is a browser-based tool for creating videos from a written script. You pick an avatar, type or paste your text, choose a voice, and the platform renders a presenter-style video without cameras, actors or studio time. It is used mainly for training material, product explainers, internal communications and localized marketing.

The current version is Synthesia 3.0, built around the Express-2 avatar engine, which generates full-body avatars with natural hand and body movement rather than static talking heads. Version 3.0 also added interactive Video Agents. Synthesia has moved to a credits system that is now the shared currency across its usage-based features, and the former 'Creator' plan has been renamed 'Pro'. The product now also sells survey tools and roleplay/learner seats alongside video creation.

The avatar catalog scales with plan: 9 AI avatars on the free Basic plan, 125+ on Starter, 180+ on Pro, and 240+ on Enterprise. Personal avatars are not available on Basic, but Starter includes 3, Pro includes 5, and Enterprise allows unlimited personal avatars. Enterprise also includes one-click translation into 140+ languages. Add-ons include a Roleplay learner seat and a Studio custom avatar built for annual-plan customers.

Pricing is tiered and credit-based. The free Basic plan is $0 per month and includes 10 minutes of video creation or dubbing per month, 500 credits per month, 9 AI avatars, a watermark, no personal avatars and no downloads. Starter is $29 per month billed monthly, or $18 per month billed annually, with 1,250 credits per month (15,000 credits per year on annual billing), roughly 12 minutes of video, 125+ avatars, 3 personal avatars, downloads, logo removal and an AI Video Assistant. Pro (formerly Creator) is $89 per month billed monthly, or $64 per month billed annually, with a base of 6,000 credits per month (scalable to higher credit tiers at additional cost), roughly 60 minutes of video, 180+ avatars, 5 personal avatars, interactive videos and branded video pages. Enterprise is custom-priced with unlimited video minutes, 240+ avatars, unlimited personal avatars, SAML/SSO and SCORM export. A Roleplay learner seat add-on is $29 per month billed monthly or $25 per month billed annually, and a Studio custom avatar is $1,000 per year for annual-plan customers.

The main limitations are the credit-based minute caps, which are tight on the Basic and Starter tiers, and the fact that avatar-led video suits explanatory content far better than cinematic or emotionally nuanced storytelling. The credits system adds a layer of complexity to understanding usage limits across features, and the most advanced capabilities, such as interactive video and higher avatar counts, sit behind the Pro and Enterprise plans.

Synthesia is a strong fit for L&D teams, HR, product marketing and anyone who needs to produce or localize a high volume of talking-head videos quickly and without a film crew. It is less suited to creators chasing highly produced, cinematic output.

before.description: Microsoft Copilot Studio is a low-code platform for building and deploying custom AI agents that connect to Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and external systems. It offers a choice of underlying models from vendors including OpenAI and Anthropic, plus computer-using agents and voice agent capabilities.
before.description_long:
Microsoft Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code environment for designing, testing and publishing AI agents. It sits inside the Power Platform and Microsoft 365 ecosystem, letting makers wire agents to enterprise data, Teams, Dynamics 365 and third-party APIs without heavy custom code.

Microsoft updates the platform on a rolling basis and publishes monthly change logs rather than a single fixed version number. Recent additions documented by Microsoft include computer-using agents reaching general availability and real-time voice agents arriving as a preview for Dynamics 365 Contact Center. A new orchestration runtime, part of a separate GitHub Copilot harness alongside the existing Standard harness, is described by Microsoft as improving response quality and reasoning.

On the capability side, the platform supports multi-agent orchestration and autonomous computer-using agents. In the Prompt Tool, makers can choose among models from vendors including OpenAI and Anthropic, with some options generally available and others offered as experimental previews.

Pricing runs on Copilot Credits. A prepaid capacity pack costs $200 per pack per month for 25,000 Copilot Credits, tenant-wide. Pay-as-you-go is also metered per credit, though the per-credit rate is not published, and requires linking an Azure subscription to the environment. A one-year prepay of Copilot Credit Commit Units can save up to 20%. A Microsoft 365 Copilot license, at $30 per user per month billed annually, includes the Standard harness for building internal agents, but publishing to external channels or using the GitHub Copilot harness requires the standalone Copilot Studio plan.

The main limitation is that there is no free production tier. A free trial exists but is time-limited and cannot publish agents; a free Azure account separately provides a $200 Azure credit. Pay-as-you-go billing requires an Azure subscription and its exact per-credit cost is not disclosed on Microsoft's pricing pages, making costs harder to forecast upfront.

Copilot Studio suits organizations already invested in Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 or Azure that want governed, low-code agents connected to their existing data. It is a weaker fit for individuals or small teams wanting a genuinely free way to ship an agent to production.

n8n is a workflow automation tool that lets you wire together apps, databases and APIs through a visual editor, with the option to drop into code when you need it. It can be self-hosted or run through n8n's managed cloud service.

The current stable release is n8n@2.42.3, published October 5, 2026, with n8n@2.43.0 available as a beta build. The older 1.x line continues to receive patches, with 1.123.83 released in late September 2026.

AI and agent workflows are a major focus: the AI Agent node supports structured tool calling against models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Mistral and Groq. Recent releases have also added dozens of new native integrations, bringing the total past 500, along with per-node retry with exponential backoff, expanded admin controls, public API access and additional enterprise authentication options.

Pricing is tiered. The self-hosted Community Edition is free, with unlimited executions and access to all integrations; n8n's cloud service offers a free trial (1,000 executions, no credit card required) but has no free ongoing plan. Paid cloud tiers include Starter and Pro, billed annually in euros, each bundling a monthly allotment of Assistant credits (1,600 on Starter, up to 9,600 on Pro). The Business tier is self-hosted only, with cloud access on a waitlist, and Enterprise pricing is custom; a startup program offers 50% off Business for companies under 20 employees.

n8n is fair-code under the Sustainable Use License rather than OSI-approved open source, which restricts commercial resale. Self-hosting puts maintenance, updates and scaling on the user. Cloud AI credits are capped and can run out on heavy agent workloads, and the highest self-hosted tier (Business) is not currently offered as a cloud plan. Workflows can also get complex enough to require a real learning curve beyond simple no-code tools.

It suits developers and technical teams who want automation they can host and audit themselves, and who want to build AI-agent workflows without stitching together separate tools.

before.description_long:
Consensus is a search tool built for academic and scientific literature. You ask a question in plain language, and it pulls relevant peer-reviewed papers, summarizes what they found, and links directly back to the sources so you can verify the claims yourself.

The product has evolved since its early days. It launched around the idea of a consensus meter that showed the percentage of studies agreeing with a claim; that feature still exists but is no longer the primary focus. As of late 2026, Consensus describes itself as an AI workspace for scientific research, with recent additions including Skills (ready-to-run research workflows), the ability to pull figures and tables directly into answers, a Research Gaps Matrix, a partnership with AAAS, and a Consensus Everywhere initiative that lets Consensus run inside ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Deep Search remains a core capability: it breaks your question into sub-questions, runs up to roughly 20 targeted searches, and synthesizes across as many as 50 papers, with a wide-coverage mode that can scan up to about 1,000. The newer MCP-based integrations extend this into other AI assistants rather than confining it to the Consensus interface.

Pricing is freemium, though exact free-tier quotas are not published on the vendor's site. Pro costs $20 per month, or $144 per year if billed annually (about $12/month). Pro includes 15 Deep Searches per month. A higher Deep plan costs $65 per month, or $540 per year if billed annually (about $45/month), and adds up to 200 Deep Searches per month on top of everything in Pro. Team and Enterprise pricing exists but is not published.

The limits are worth knowing. Coverage skews toward what is indexed, and some records are abstract-level only; like any AI summarizer, it can flatten nuance, so you still need to read primary sources for anything high-stakes. Note also that an unrelated sales-demo product at goconsensus.com shares the name and costs $600-$1,250/mo; it is not this tool.

It suits researchers, students, clinicians, and analysts who want grounded, citable answers from the literature and are comfortable verifying against the originals rather than trusting a summary at face value.

The headline feature is Figma Make, which turns a written prompt into a working, interactive prototype and can connect to a Supabase backend to build functional apps. Figma's pricing page also now lists a Figma agent for on-canvas chat-based design generation, a Figma MCP server with MCP connectors, and a newer product called Figma Weave for AI workflows covering imagery, video and audio.

Figma moved these AI features out of a free, effectively unlimited beta and into a metered AI-credit economy shared across all its AI tools. New AI add-ons are now available across all plans.

Capability-wise, this consolidates most of Figma's AI story in one place: generate a first draft, iterate with Make, produce or edit images, rewrite and translate copy, chat with an on-canvas agent, and hand off to real design files. Credits are consumed per action, though the exact cost per action is not published.

The free Starter plan is capped at 150 credits per day and 500 per month, with unlimited drafts. Organization seats are $55 (Full), $25 (Dev) and $5 (Collab) per month, billed annually, adding up to 3,500 credits. Enterprise seats are $90 (Full), $35 (Dev) and $5 (Collab) per month, billed annually, adding up to 4,250 credits. Beyond the monthly allotment, additional usage is available as a pay-as-you-go or subscription-based credit add-on.

The main limitation is exactly that metering: heavy AI users can burn through credits quickly, and the daily cap on the free tier makes sustained experimentation hard. Output quality from Make and First Draft is a starting point, not a finished design, and still needs a designer's hand. Billing periods for Professional-tier pricing are also unclear on Figma's own pricing page, making cost comparisons harder.

Figma AI makes the most sense for teams already living in Figma who want AI woven into their existing files rather than a separate tool. If you rarely touch AI, the free allotment may be enough; if AI is central to your workflow, budget for a paid tier and possible overage.
